q: Which file extension is normally given to a C source file?
x: C source programs are saved with the extension .c. A .h file is a header file, and .exe is the executable made after compiling and linking.

q: Which header file must be included to use the library functions `sqrt()` and `pow()`?
x: The mathematical functions such as sqrt() and pow() are declared in math.h. stdio.h declares input/output functions such as printf() and scanf().

q: What is the C program called as the programmer writes it, before any translation?
x: The program typed in the editor is the source code (source program). Object code is what the compiler produces from it, and the executable is made by the linker.

q: Where are preprocessor directives such as `#include` normally written in a C program?
o: Inside main(), after the last statement
Only after the closing brace of main()
Inside the format string of printf()
At the top of the file, before main()
x: Directives are usually placed at the start of the program so that their effect, such as declaring printf(), applies to all the code below. Inside a format string, # is just a printed character.

q: A program compiles and links without errors. While it is running, the user enters 0, the program divides by this value and stops abnormally. What kind of error is this?
x: The program was translated successfully and failed only while executing, so it is a run-time error. A syntax error would have been reported by the compiler before any executable was made.

q: A program has `#define RATE 5` at the top and the statement `tax = price * RATE;` in main(). What does the preprocessor do with RATE?
o: It creates an int variable RATE in memory that holds 5
It replaces RATE with 5 before the compiler sees the statement
It asks the user to enter a value for RATE at run time
It leaves RATE for the linker to find in a library
x: #define makes a macro: the preprocessor substitutes the text 5 for RATE, so the compiler sees tax = price * 5;. No variable is created and nothing happens at run time.

q: Why must a C program be translated before the computer can run it?
o: The CPU can execute only assembly-language instructions
The CPU can execute only machine-language instructions
Translation is needed only to remove the comments
Translation is needed only to check the spelling of variables
x: A processor understands only machine code (binary instructions), so C statements must be compiled into it. Assembly language also has to be translated, by an assembler.

q: Which preprocessor line is written correctly?
x: A directive starts with #, the word include is in lower case because C is case-sensitive, and a standard header's name goes in angle brackets, not round ones. Without the angle brackets or the #, the line is an error.

q: A program has been compiled and linked into an executable file. The source file is then deleted. What happens when the executable file is run?
o: It fails, because the source file is read each time it runs
It runs normally, since it no longer needs the source file
It runs only after the program is compiled again
It shows the source code instead of running
x: The executable already contains the machine code, so the source file is not needed to run it. The source is needed only to change and recompile the program.

q: A program will be run many times without changes. What is an advantage of compiling it rather than running it through an interpreter?
o: It can be changed without being translated again
Errors are reported one line at a time while it runs
No translator program is needed at all
Once compiled, it runs without being translated again each time
x: A compiler translates the whole program once into an executable, which then runs directly and faster. An interpreter must translate the statements again every time the program runs.

q: A C program has a syntax error in one line. What happens when it is compiled?
o: The compiler skips that line and makes the object file
The linker corrects the error automatically
The compiler reports the error and no object file is made until it is fixed
The program runs and stops only when it reaches that line
x: The compiler cannot translate code that breaks the rules of C, so it lists the error and does not produce object code. The linker only joins object code; it never fixes source errors.

q: Which part of an IDE lets the programmer run a program one statement at a time and watch the values of variables change?
x: A debugger lets the programmer step through statements and inspect variables to find logical errors. The linker and loader prepare and load the program but do not step through it.

q: Which is a correct difference between `#define N 10` and `const int n = 10;`?
o: N is replaced by 10 before compiling and has no data type; n is an int whose value cannot change
N can be changed later by an assignment; n cannot
N is stored in memory as an int; n is replaced by 10 before compiling
There is no difference except the spelling of the names
x: A macro is plain text substitution done by the preprocessor, so N has no type and no memory. The const declaration makes a real int variable that the compiler will not let the program change.

q: What does a header file such as `stdio.h` mainly contain?
o: The complete machine code of printf and scanf
Declarations of library functions such as printf, and macro definitions
The main() function of every program
The finished executable file of the program
x: A header file is source text with function declarations (prototypes) and macros. The machine code of printf is in the compiled library, which the linker joins to the program.

q: Which match of a stage with what it produces is WRONG?
x: The loader produces no file: it copies the executable into main memory to run it. The preprocessor expands the source, the compiler makes object code, and the linker builds the executable.

q: A source file has three `#include` lines and one `#define` line. After preprocessing, how many of these four lines are still present, unchanged, in the code passed to the compiler?
x: The preprocessor replaces each #include line with the header's contents and uses the #define line to replace the macro name, then drops it. So none of the four directive lines reach the compiler as written.

q: Which data type is used to store a single character such as 'k'?
x: char holds one character (stored as its character code). float and double are for numbers with fractional parts.

q: Which keyword declares a variable for a floating-point number with double precision?
x: double gives about twice the precision of float. long and int are integer types and cannot hold fractions.
Each of n-- and --n, written as a statement on its own, lowers n by 1: 8 → 7 → 6. The prefix/postfix difference matters only when the value is used inside a larger expression.

q: Which of these is a valid character constant in C?
x: A character constant is one character in single quotes, 'k'. "k" is a string constant, k without quotes is an identifier, and 'k is missing its closing quote.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d", 20 - 14 % 4 * 2);
```
x: % and * have higher precedence than - and are done left to right: 14 % 4 = 2, then 2 * 2 = 4, then 20 - 4 = 16. Doing the subtraction first, (20 - 14) % 4 * 2, would give 4.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d %d", 7 != 7, 4 <= 4);
```
x: A relational expression gives 1 when true and 0 when false. 7 != 7 is false (0), and 4 <= 4 is true (1) because <= includes equality.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d", (2 + 3) * 4 % 7);
```
x: The brackets come first: 5; then * and %, which have equal precedence, go left to right: 5 * 4 = 20, 20 % 7 = 6. Without the brackets, 2 + 12 % 7 would give 7.
347 / 10 = 34 with integer division, and 34 % 10 = 4, the tens digit; 347 % 10 = 7, the units digit. Stopping at n / 10 gives 34.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.1f", 2.5e2);
```
x: 2.5e2 means 2.5 × 10² = 250, printed with one decimal place as 250.0. 0.025 would be 2.5e-2.
The variables are set in order: a = 3, then b = 3 + 2 = 5, then c = 3 × 5 = 15. 9 would come from using a * a.

q: Among the operators `+`, `*`, `=` and `&&`, which has the highest precedence?
x: Multiplication is done before addition, both arithmetic operators come before the logical &&, and assignment = has the lowest precedence of the four.
An assignment is also an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = 4) stores 4 in x and gives 4; then y = 4 + 3 = 7.
x *= 2 + 3 means x = x * (2 + 3), because the whole right side is worked out first: 4 × 5 = 20. Reading it as x * 2 + 3 gives the tempting 11.
An integer constant that starts with 0 is octal, so 012 = 1 × 8 + 2 = 10, and x + 1 = 11 in decimal. Reading 012 as decimal twelve gives 13.
The digit characters have consecutive codes ('0' is 48, '7' is 55), so '7' - '0' = 7 and d * 2 = 14. Doubling the code of '7' itself gives 110.
&& has higher precedence than ||, so the first is 1 || (0 && 0) = 1 || 0 = 1. The brackets in the second force (1 || 0) first, giving 1 && 0 = 0.

q: Which escape sequence moves the cursor to the next tab stop?
x: \t is the horizontal tab. \n is a new line, \b a backspace and \a an alert (beep).

q: Which format specifier is used in printf to print a single character?
x: %c prints one character. %s prints a whole string, %d an integer and %f a floating-point number.

q: Which format specifier prints a string such as "Lahore"?
x: %s prints the characters of a string until its terminating null character. %c would print only one character.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("Sum=%d, Avg=%.1f", 12, 12 / 5.0);
```
x: Ordinary characters are printed as they are and each specifier is replaced by its value; 12 / 5.0 = 2.4 because 5.0 is a floating-point constant. Integer division would give 2, shown as 2.0.
%d reads 5 into n and %f reads 2.5 into x; n * x = 12.5, printed with one decimal place. 7.5 would be n + x.

q: In `char name[20]; scanf("%s", name);` why is no & written before name?
o: Strings can be read only from files, not from the keyboard
The & sign is needed only with printf
The name of an array already gives the address of the array
scanf first reads the string into a temporary variable
x: scanf needs addresses, and an array's name stands for the address of its first element, so name is already an address. For a plain int variable the & is needed to give its address.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.3f", 1.0 / 8);
```
x: 1.0 / 8 is a floating-point division giving 0.125, and %.3f prints exactly three decimal places. 0.000 would come from integer division 1 / 8 = 0, which does not happen because 1.0 is not an integer.

q: Which format specifier prints a value of type `long int`?
x: The l modifier with d, %ld, is for long int. %lf is used with scanf for a double, and plain %d is for int.

q: Which character constant stores a single quote (')?
x: Inside single quotes, a single quote must be written with the escape sequence \'. Three quotes in a row are an error, "'" is a string rather than a character constant, and '\"' is the double quote.

o: Nothing, it waits for another line
x: The first scanf reads 3 and leaves " 9" waiting; the second %d skips the space and reads 9, so b - a = 9 - 3 = 6. A space separates numbers just as Enter does.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.1f", 9 / 2.0 + 1);
```
x: 9 / 2.0 = 4.5 because 2.0 is a floating-point constant, then 4.5 + 1 = 5.5. Integer division 9 / 2 = 4 would give 5.0.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("[%2d]", 12345);
```
x: A field width is a minimum: a number that needs more places is printed in full, so all five digits appear. The width never cuts digits off.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%d", 3, 4);
```
x: printf prints according to its format string, which has one %d, so it prints 3; the extra argument 4 is not used. It is not a compile error, though a compiler may warn about it.
%d reads 7 and stops at the space; %c does not skip spaces, so it reads the space character into ch, and [ ] is printed. To read k, the format would need a space before %c.
%2d reads at most 2 digits, so a = 12; the next %d reads the remaining digits, so b = 345. Without the width, a would take all five digits.

q:
What is printed?
```
printf("a\\nb");
```
o: a and b on two separate lines
x: \\ is the escape sequence for one backslash, so the characters printed are a, \, n, b: a\nb on one line. There is no \n escape here, so no new line is started.
